==Demographics==
=== Immigration ===
{{Main|Immigration to Australia}}
[[File:StateLibQld 1 110096 Drawing of migrants disembarking from a ship, ca. 1885.jpg|thumb|upright|Migrants to Australia disembarking from a ship, 1885]]

Since 1945, more than 7 million people have settled in Australia. From the late 1970s, there was a significant increase in immigration from Asian and other non-European countries, making Australia a [[Multiculturalism in Australia|multicultural country]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Latestproducts/3412.0Main+Features52015-16?opendocument&tabname=Summary&prodno=3412.0&issue=2015-16&num=&view=|title=Main Features – Net Overseas Migration|first=c=AU; o=Commonwealth of Australia; ou=Australian Bureau of|last=Statistics|website=www.abs.gov.au|access-date=10 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171010010130/http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Latestproducts/3412.0Main+Features52015-16?opendocument&tabname=Summary&prodno=3412.0&issue=2015-16&num=&view=|archive-date=10 October 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> Sydney is the most [[multicultural]] city in Oceania, having more than 250 different languages spoken, with about 40 percent of residents speaking a [[Languages Other Than English|language other than English]] at home.<ref>{{cite news|work=The Sydney Morning Herald|date=2014|url=https://www.smh.com.au/data-point/sydney-languages|title=Sydney's melting pot of language|access-date=13 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140923055934/http://www.smh.com.au/data-point/sydney-languages|archive-date=23 September 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> Furthermore, 36 percent of the population reported having been [[foreign born|born overseas]], with top countries being [[Italy]], [[Lebanon]], [[Vietnam]] and [[Iraq]], among others.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/news/inquirer/census-2016-migrants-make-a-cosmopolitan-country/news-story/da01bec138fc8600ea7bb84d1844ea80|title=Census 2016: Migrants make a cosmopolitan country|work=The Australian|date=15 July 2017|url-access=subscription|access-date=16 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|publisher=.id|date=2014|url=http://profile.id.com.au/sydney/population|title=Population, dwellings, and ethnicity|access-date=27 July 2014}}</ref> [[Melbourne]] is also fairly multicultural, having the largest [[Greek community of Melbourne|Greek-speaking]] population outside of [[Europe]],<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.oecd.org/gov/regional-policy/50242959.pdf | title=Regional, rural and urban development - OECD }}</ref> and the second largest [[Asian Australians|Asian]] population in Australia after Sydney.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vicnet.net.au/community/ethnic/indian/ |title=Vicnet Directory Indian Community |publisher=Vicnet |access-date=2 October 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080928011559/http://www.vicnet.net.au/community/ethnic/indian/ |archive-date=28 September 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vicnet.net.au/community/ethnic/srilankan/ |title=Vicnet Directory Sri Lankan Community |publisher=Vicnet |access-date=2 October 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081016054206/http://www.vicnet.net.au/community/ethnic/srilankan/ |archive-date=16 October 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724113628/http://www.yarranet.net.au/~acacia/vietcom.htm |archive-date=24 July 2008 }}</ref>

===Religion===
{{Main|Religion in Australia|Religion in Papua New Guinea}}

[[Christianity]] is the predominant religion in the continent, although large proportions of Australians belong to [[Irreligion|no religion]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20130815184022/http://wwwgordonconwell.com/netcommunity/CSGCResources/ChristianityinitsGlobalContext.pdf Christianity in its Global Context, 1970–2020 Society, Religion, and Mission], Center for the Study of Global Christianity</ref> Other religions in the region include [[Islam]], [[Buddhism]] and [[Hinduism]], which are prominent [[minority religion]]s in Australia. Traditional religions are often [[Animism|animist]], found in New Guinea. [[Islam]] is widespread in the [[Indonesian New Guinea]].<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Latestproducts/2071.0Main%20Features902012%E2%80%932013 |work = 2071.0 – Reflecting a Nation: Stories from the 2011 Census, 2012–2013 |title = Cultural diversity in Australia |date = 21 June 2012 |publisher = Australian Bureau of Statistics |access-date = 27 June 2012 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160425232111/http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Latestproducts/2071.0Main%20Features902012%E2%80%932013 |archive-date = 25 April 2016 }}</ref> Many Papuans [[Religious syncretism|combine their Christian faith with traditional indigenous beliefs and practices]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://2001-2009.state.gov/g/drl/rls/irf/2003/24317.htm | access-date = 23 March 2006 | title = US Department of State ''International Religious Freedom Report 2003''}}</ref>

===Languages===
{{Main|Languages of Australia|Languages of Papua New Guinea|Languages of Indonesia}}

"[[Aboriginal Australian languages]]", including the large [[Pama–Nyungan]] family, "[[Papuan languages]]" of [[New Guinea]] and neighbouring islands, including the large [[Trans–New Guinea]] family, and "[[Tasmanian languages]]" are generic terms for the native languages of the continent other than those of [[Austronesian languages|Austronesian]] family.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Silva|first=Diego B.|date=2019|title=Language policy in Oceania|journal=Alfa|volume=63 |pages=317–347 |doi=10.1590/1981-5794-1909-4 |s2cid=204627919 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Predominant languages include [[English language|English]] in Australia, [[Tok Pisin]] in Papua New Guinea, and [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]] (Malay) in Indonesian New Guinea. [[Immigration to Australia]] have brought overseas languages such as [[Italian language|Italian]], [[Greek language|Greek]], [[Arabic language|Arabic]], [[Filipino language|Filipino]], [[Mandarin language|Mandarin]], [[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese]] and [[Spanish language|Spanish]], among others.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Lookup/2071.0main+features902012-2013|title=Main Features – Cultural Diversity in Australia|first=c=AU; o=Commonwealth of Australia; ou=Australian Bureau of|last=Statistics|website=www.abs.gov.au|date=21 June 2012}}</ref> Contact between Austronesian and Papuan resulted in several instances in [[mixed language]]s such as [[Maisin language|Maisin]]. [[Tok Pisin]] is an English [[creole language]] spoken in Papua New Guinea.<ref>{{cite news|author1=A.V.|title=Papua New Guinea's incredible linguistic diversity|url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/economist-explains/2017/07/economist-explains-14|access-date=20 July 2017|newspaper=[[The Economist]]|date=24 July 2017}}</ref> Papua New Guinea has more languages than any other country,<ref name="Seetharaman-2017"/> with over 820 indigenous languages, representing 12% of the world's total, but most have fewer than 1,000 speakers.<ref>[http://www.ethnologue.com/country/PG Papua New Guinea], Ethnologue</ref>

==Culture==
{{Main|Culture of Australia|Culture of Papua New Guinea|Australian Aboriginal culture}}

Since 1788, the primary influence behind Australian culture has been [[Anglo-Celtic]] [[Western culture]], with some [[Indigenous Australians|Indigenous]] influences.<ref>[[#Jupp|Jupp]], pp. 796–802.</ref><ref>[[#Teo|Teo and White]], pp. 118–20.</ref><ref name="Teo-2003">{{Cite book|last1=Teo|first1=Hsu-Ming|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/1120581500|title=Cultural history in Australia|last2=White|first2=Richard|date=2003|publisher=UNSW Press|isbn=0-86840-589-2|oclc=1120581500}}</ref> The divergence and evolution that has occurred in the ensuing centuries has resulted in a distinctive Australian culture.<ref>{{Harvnb|Davison|Hirst|Macintyre|1998|pages=98–9}}</ref><ref>[[#Teo|Teo and White]], pp. 125–27.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|date=1 January 2001|editor-last=Davison|editor-first=Graeme|editor2-last=Hirst|editor2-first=John|editor3-last=Macintyre|editor3-first=Stuart|title=The Oxford Companion to Australian History|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/acref/9780195515039.001.0001|doi=10.1093/acref/9780195515039.001.0001|isbn=978-0-19-551503-9}}</ref> Since the mid-20th century, [[Culture of the United States|American popular culture]] has strongly influenced Australia, particularly through television and cinema.<ref name="Teo and White">[[#Teo|Teo and White]], pp. 121–23.</ref><ref name="Teo-2003" /> Other cultural influences come from neighbouring Asian countries, and through large-scale immigration from non-English-speaking nations.<ref name="Teo and White" /><ref name="Teo-2003" /><ref>[[#Jupp|Jupp]], pp. 808–12, 74–77.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=James.|first=Jupp|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/760277445|title=The Australian people : an encyclopedia of the nation, its people and their origins|date=2001|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0-521-80789-1|oclc=760277445}}</ref> The [[Australian Museum]] in Sydney and the [[National Gallery of Victoria]] in Melbourne are the oldest and [[List of largest art museums|largest]] [[museum]]s in the continent, as well as in [[Oceania]].<ref>Australian Museum, ''A Short History of the Australian Museum'', http://australianmuseum.net.au/A-short-history-of-the-Australian-Museum</ref><ref>National Gallery of Victoria – Victorian Heritage Register</ref> Sydney's [[Sydney New Year's Eve|New Year's Eve]] celebrations are the largest in the continent.<ref>{{cite news|last=Kaur |first=Jaskiran |date=2013 |url=http://au.ibtimes.com/articles/531947/20131227/party-new-year-s-eve-australia-sydney.htm |title=Where to party in Australia on New Year's Eve |work=International Business Times|access-date=27 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140708231528/http://au.ibtimes.com/articles/531947/20131227/party-new-year-s-eve-australia-sydney.htm |archive-date=8 July 2014 }}</ref>

It is estimated that more than 7,000 different cultural groups exist in Papua New Guinea, and most groups have their own language. Because of this diversity, in which they take pride, many different styles of cultural expression have emerged; each group has created its own expressive forms in [[art]], [[performance art]], [[weapon]]ry, [[costume]]s and [[architecture]]. Papua New Guinea is one of the few cultures in Oceania to practice the tradition of [[bride price]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Papua New Guinea – culture |work=Datec Pty Ltd |url=http://www.datec.com.au/png/culture.htm |access-date=16 December 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990210114159/http://www.datec.com.au/png/culture.htm |archive-date=10 February 1999}}</ref> In particular, Papua New Guinea is world-famous for carved wooden [[sculpture]]: masks, canoes, story-boards.

Australia has a tradition of Aboriginal art which is thousands of years old, the best known forms being rock art and [[bark painting]]. Evidence of [[Aboriginal art]] in Australia can be traced back at least 30,000 years.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cultureandrecreation.gov.au/articles/indigenous/art/index.htm|title=Australian Indigenous art|work=Australian Culture and Recreation Portal|publisher=Australia Government|date=21 December 2007|access-date=26 September 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100416144209/http://www.cultureandrecreation.gov.au/articles/indigenous/art/index.htm|archive-date=16 April 2010}}</ref> Examples of ancient Aboriginal rock artworks can be found throughout the continent—notably in national parks such as those of the [[UNESCO]] listed sites at [[Uluru]] and [[Kakadu National Park]] in the Northern Territory, but also within [[Sydney rock engravings|protected parks in urban areas]] such as at [[Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park]] in Sydney.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://parksaustralia.gov.au/kakadu/people/rock-art.html|title=Kakadu: Rock art|work=parksaustralia.gov.au|access-date=29 January 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://parksaustralia.gov.au/uluru/people-place/rock-art.html|title=Uluru-Kata Tjuta: Rock art|publisher=parksaustralia.gov.au|access-date=29 January 2017}}</ref> Aboriginal culture includes a number of practices and ceremonies centered on a belief in the [[Dreamtime]]. Reverence for the land and oral traditions are emphasised.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalparks.nsw.gov.au/things-to-do/Walking-tracks/Aboriginal-Heritage-walk|title=Aboriginal Heritage walk: Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park|work=nationalparks.nsw.gov.au|access-date=29 January 2017}}</ref>

===Sport===
{{Main|Sport in Australia|Sport in Papua New Guinea}}
[[Image:Png mosquitos 2008 international cup.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|[[Papua New Guinea national Australian rules football team|Papua New Guinea's national team]] at the [[2008 International Cup]] (Australian rules football) in Melbourne]]

Popular sports in Papua New Guinea include various codes of [[football]] ([[rugby league]], [[rugby union]], [[soccer]], and [[Australian rules football]]), [[cricket]], [[volleyball]], [[softball]], [[netball]], and [[basketball]]. Other [[Olympic Games|Olympic sports]] are also gaining popularity, such as [[boxing]] and [[Olympic weightlifting|weightlifting]]. [[Rugby league]] is the most popular sport in Papua New Guinea (especially in the highlands), which also unofficially holds the title as the ''national sport''.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/rugby_league/7671217.stm|title=PNG vow to upset World Cup odds|date=15 October 2008|work=Rugby League|publisher=BBC|access-date=3 July 2009|quote=But it would still be one of the biggest shocks in [[Rugby League World Cup Records|World Cup history]] if Papua New Guinea – ''the only country to have Rugby League as its national Sport'' – were to qualify for the last 4.}}</ref> The most popular sport in Australia is [[cricket]], the most popular sport among Australian women is [[netball]], while [[Australian rules football]] is the most popular sport in terms of spectatorship and television ratings.<ref>''Australia (Countries & Cultures)'', Tracey Boraas, Capstone Press (2002), Page 54 {{ISBN|0736810757}}</ref><ref>''Planet Sport'', Kath Woodward, 2012 p. 85 {{ISBN|041568112X}}</ref><ref>Australia (Cultures of the World), Vijeya Rajendra, Sundran Rajendra, 2002, p. 101 {{ISBN|0761414738}}</ref> Australia has hosted two Summer Olympic Games: [[1956 Summer Olympics|Melbourne 1956]] and [[2000 Summer Olympics|Sydney 2000]]. Australia has also hosted five editions of the [[Commonwealth Games]] ([[1938 British Empire Games|Sydney 1938]], [[1962 British Empire and Commonwealth Games|Perth 1962]], [[1982 Commonwealth Games|Brisbane 1982]], [[2006 Commonwealth Games|Melbourne 2006]], and [[2018 Commonwealth Games|Gold Coast 2018]]). In 2006 [[Socceroo|Australia]] joined the [[Asian Football Confederation]] and qualified for the 2010 and [[2014 FIFA World Cup|2014]] World Cups as an Asian entrant.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fifa.com/worldcup/tournament/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090228220920/http://www.fifa.com/worldcup/tournament/index.html|archive-date=28 February 2009 |title=FIFA world cup 2010 – qualifying rounds and places available by confederation |publisher=Fifa.com |date=3 April 2009 |access-date=17 April 2009}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Boundaries between the continents
======================================================================

{{Short description|Geographical convention}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2020}}
[[File:Continents vide couleurs.png|thumb|300px|Color-coded map of continents:<br />
{{legend0|#0f0}}{{legend0|#0a5}}[[Americas]]<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{{legend0|#0f0}}[[North America]]<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{{legend0|#0a5}}[[South America]]<br />
{{legend0|#fed52e}}{{legend0|#f33e01}}{{legend0|#c10000}}[[Afro-Eurasia]]<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{{legend0|#fed52e}}[[Africa]]<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{{legend0|#f33e01}}{{legend0|#c10000}}[[Eurasia]]<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{{legend0|#c10000}}[[Europe]]<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{{legend0|#f33e01}}[[Asia]]<br />
{{legend0|#c04080}} [[Oceania]]<br />
{{legend0|#0040ff}}[[Antarctica]]]]
[[File:Island nations.svg|thumb|300px|Map of [[island country|island countries]]: These states are not located on any continent-sized landmass, but they are usually grouped geographically with a neighbouring continent.]]

Determining the boundaries between the [[continent]]s is generally a matter of [[geography|geographical]] convention and consensus. 

Several slightly different conventions are in use. The number of continents is most commonly considered seven (in [[list of countries by English-speaking population|English-speaking countries]]) but may range as low as four when [[Afro-Eurasia]] and the [[Americas]] are both considered as single continents.<ref name="McColl">{{cite encyclopedia |title=continents |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of World Geography |volume=1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DJgnebGbAB8C&pg=PA215 |editor=R.W. McColl |year=2005 |publisher=Facts on File, Inc. |isbn=978-0-8160-7229-3 |page=215 |access-date=26 June 2012 |quote=And since Africa and Asia are connected at the Suez Peninsula, Europe, Africa, and Asia are sometimes combined as Afro-Eurasia or Eurafrasia. The International Olympic Committee's official flag, containing [...] the single continent of America (North and South America being connected as the Isthmus of Panama).}}</ref> 

An [[island]] can be considered to be [[Continent#Extent|associated with a given continent]] by either lying on the continent's adjacent [[continental shelf]] (e.g. [[Singapore]], the [[British Isles]]) or being a part of a [[microcontinent]] on the same [[list of tectonic plates|principal tectonic plate]] (e.g. [[Madagascar]] and [[Seychelles]]). An [[island]] can also be entirely [[Island#Geology|oceanic]] while still being associated with a continent by [[geology]] (e.g. [[Bermuda]], the [[Australian Indian Ocean Territories]]) or by common [[geopolitics|geopolitical]] convention (e.g. [[Ascension Island]], the [[South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands#South Sandwich Islands|South Sandwich Islands]]). Another example is the grouping into [[Oceania]] of the [[list of islands in the Pacific Ocean|Pacific Islands]] with [[Australia (continent)|Australia]] and [[Zealandia]].

There are three overland boundaries subject to definition:
* between [[Africa]] and [[Asia]] (dividing Afro-Eurasia into Africa and [[Eurasia]]): at the [[Isthmus of Suez]];
* between Asia and [[Europe]] (dividing [[Eurasia]]): along the [[Turkish Straits]], the [[Caucasus]], and the [[Urals]] and the [[Ural (river)|Ural River]] (historically also north of the Caucasus, along the [[Kuma–Manych Depression]] or along the [[Don (river)|Don River]]);
* between [[North America]] and [[South America]] (dividing the [[Americas]]): at some point on the [[Isthmus of Panama]], with the most common demarcation in atlases and other sources following the [[Serranía del Darién|Darién Mountains]] watershed along the [[Colombia–Panama border]] where the isthmus meets the South American continent (see [[Darién Gap]]).

While today the [[isthmus]] between Asia and Africa is navigable via the [[Suez Canal]], and that between North and [[South America]] via the [[Panama Canal]], these artificial channels are not generally accepted as continent-defining boundaries in themselves. The Suez Canal happens to traverse the Isthmus of Suez between the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Red Sea]], dividing Africa and Asia. The continental boundaries are considered to be within the very narrow land connections joining the continents.

The remaining boundaries concern the association of islands and archipelagos with specific continents, notably:
* the delineation between Africa, Asia, and Europe in the [[Mediterranean Sea]];
* the delineation between Asia and Europe in the [[Arctic Ocean]];
* the delineation between Europe and North America in the North [[Atlantic Ocean]];
* the delineation between North and South America in the [[Caribbean Sea]];
* the delineation of [[Antarctica]] from Africa, [[Australia (continent)|Australia]], and South America in the [[Indian Ocean|Indian]], South [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]], and South Atlantic oceans, respectively (referred to collectively by some geographers as the [[Southern Ocean]] or the Antarctic Ocean);
* the delineation of Asia from [[Australia (continent)|Australia]] in the [[Ceram Sea]], [[Arafura Sea]], [[Timor Sea]], [[Halmahera Sea]], and the [[Wallacea]]n region of the [[Indonesian Archipelago]]
* the delineation of Asia from North America in the North Pacific Ocean.

==Africa and Asia==
[[File:TransAfrica.PNG|thumb|
{{legend|#FF0000|African part of Egypt}}
{{legend|#FFA500|Asian part of Egypt}}
{{legend|#C0C0C0|Rest of Africa}}
{{legend|#FFFF00|Rest of Asia}}]]

Historically in [[Greco-Roman geography]], "Africa" meant [[ancient Libya]], and its eastern extent was taken to be around [[Marmarica]], at the ''[[Catabathmus Magnus]].'' This was not considered a continent. As wider knowledge of geography developed, the shape of the African landmass (and Egypt's "natural" inclusion in that landmass) became apparent. In 1806, [[William George Browne]] still titled his travelogue ''Travels in Africa, Egypt, and Syria''. Similarly, [[James Bruce]] in 1835 published ''Travels through part of Africa, Syria, Egypt, and Arabia''. On the other hand, as early as 1670 [[John Ogilby]] under the title ''Africa'' published ''"an accurate Description of the Regions of Egypt, Barbary, Libya, and Billedulgerid, the Land of Negroes, Guinea, Æthiopia, and the Abyssines, with all the adjacent Islands, either in the Mediterranean, Atlantic, Southern, or Oriental Seas, belonging thereunto"''.{{cn|date=March 2026}}

The usual line taken to divide Africa from Asia today is at the [[Isthmus of Suez]], the narrowest gap between the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Gulf of Suez]], the route today followed by the [[Suez Canal]]. This makes the [[Sinai Peninsula]] geographically Asian, and [[Egypt]] a transcontinental country. Less than 2% of the Egyptian population live on the Sinai Peninsula, and hence Egypt, even though technically transcontinental, is usually considered an African country entirely and not partly Asian. But when discussing the geopolitical region of the [[Middle East and North Africa]], Egypt is usually grouped with the Western Asian countries as part of the [[Middle East]], while Egypt's western neighbor [[Libya]] is grouped with the remaining North African countries as the [[Maghreb]]. Both are members of the [[African Union]]. However, the geological boundary is located further to the east, along the [[Gulf of Aqaba]] and the [[Dead Sea Transform]], with the Sinai Peninsula, [[Israel]], [[Palestine (state)|Palestine]], much of [[Lebanon]], and the coastal governorates of Syria being located on the [[African Plate]].{{cn|date=March 2026}}

The [[Comoros]], [[Madagascar]], [[Mauritius]], and [[Seychelles]] are island countries in the [[Indian Ocean]] which are nominally associated with Africa.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Abegunrin |first1=Olayiwola |last2=Manyeruke |first2=Charity |title=China's Power in Africa: A New Global Order |date=2019 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |page=10 |isbn=978-3-030-21994-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4ci1DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22madAGASCAR+IN+EAST+AFRICA%22&pg=PA10 |access-date=11 August 2022 |quote=For instance, in one of the only two instances when China was ruled by a foreign dynasty, Yuan Dynasty ambassadors, this time Mongols, traveled to Madagascar in East Africa.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/comoros/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110042946/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/comoros |archive-date=10 January 2021 |title=Comoros |date=11 July 2022 |publisher=Central Intelligence Agency |via=CIA.gov}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.uneca.org/sites/default/files/SROs/Eastern-Africa/ICSOE-24/full_report_services_trade_report_.pdf |title=The Economic and Social Impacts of the COVID-19 Crisis on Eastern Africa |website=Uneca.org |access-date=26 July 2022}}</ref> The [[Socotra Governorate|Socotra Archipelago]] may be considered African as it lies on its continental shelf; however, it is politically a part of [[Yemen]], an Asian country.{{cn|date=March 2026}}

==Africa and Europe==
[[File:Mediterranean Relief.jpg|left|thumb|upright=1.35|The Mediterranean Sea, between Africa and Europe]]
[[File:Makaronesia.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|The Atlantic Ocean around the plate boundaries (text is in [[Finnish language|Finnish]])]]

The [[Africa]]n and [[Europe]]an mainlands are non-contiguous, and the delineation between these continents is thus merely a question of which islands are to be associated with which [[continent]].{{cn|date=March 2026}}

The Portuguese Atlantic island possession of the [[Azores]] is {{convert|1368|km|abbr=on}} from Europe and {{convert|1507|km|abbr=on}} from Africa, and is sometimes grouped with Europe. By contrast, the [[Canary Islands]] and the [[Madeira]] islands (the latter of which also include the [[Desertas Islands]] and the [[Savage Islands]]) off the Atlantic coast of [[Morocco]] are much closer to, and usually grouped with, Africa; the [[Canary Islands]] are only {{convert|100|km|abbr=on}} from the African mainland at their closest point but {{convert|945|km|abbr=on}} from the European mainland, while Madeira is {{convert|520|km|abbr=on}} from the African mainland and {{convert|1000|km|abbr=on}} from the European mainland.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Canary Islands |url=http://spainforvisitors.com/sections/canaryislands.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121225123213/http://spainforvisitors.com/sections/canaryislands.htm |archive-date=25 December 2012 |access-date=15 October 2012}}; {{cite web |title=Countries of Africa |url=http://listofafricancountries.com |access-date=14 June 2016}}</ref> In his 1895 book ''Africa: Volume 2'', author Augustus Henry Keane remarked, "In the North Atlantic there are four insular groups — Madeira, the Canaries, [[Cape Verde]], and the Azores — which are usually assigned to Africa, although the Canaries and Cape Verde alone belong geographically to that continent, the Azores are lost, so to say, in mid-Atlantic."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Keane |first1=Augustus Henry |title=Africa: Volume 2 |date=1895 |publisher=The University of California |page=636 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gA5FAAAAIAAJ&dq=%22azores%22+%22geographically%22+%22africa%22&pg=PA636 |access-date=12 March 2022}}</ref>

The Mediterranean [[island country]] of [[Malta]] was considered a part of Africa for centuries.<ref>Falconer, William; Falconer, Thomas. [https://books.google.com/books?id=B3Q29kWRdtgC&pg=PA50 ''Dissertation on St. Paul's Voyage''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170327020614/https://books.google.com/books?id=B3Q29kWRdtgC&pg=PA50 |date=2017}}, BiblioLife (BiblioBazaar), 1872. (1817.), p. 50, {{ISBN|1-113-68809-2}} ''These islands Pliny, as well as Strabo and Ptolemy, included in the African sea''</ref> However, it is much closer to the coast of [[Sicily]] (a distance of about {{convert|81|km|abbr=on}}) than it is to the African mainland (roughly {{convert|288|km|abbr=on}} away).<ref>{{cite web |last=Bonello |first=Giovanni |date=2024-12-29 |title=A 1668 guidebook to Malta in Africa |url=https://timesofmalta.com/article/a-1668-guidebook-malta-africa.1102908 |access-date=2025-08-05 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-gb}}</ref> The nearby Italian island of [[Lampedusa]] (principal island of the [[Pelagian Islands]]) is {{convert|207|km|abbr=on}} from Sicily while just {{convert|127|km|abbr=on}} from the African mainland; similarly, [[Pantelleria]] is {{convert|100|km|abbr=on}} from Sicily and just {{convert|71|km|abbr=on}} from the African mainland. All of these Mediterranean islands, including Malta and Sicily, are actually located on the [[African Plate]], and could be considered part of the African continent geologically.<ref name="na">{{cite book |last1=Hutt |first1=Graham |title=North Africa |date=2010 |publisher=Imray, Laurie, Norie and Wilson Limited |page=265 |isbn=978-1-84623-883-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HxGQDwAAQBAJ&dq=Lampione+%22africa%22&pg=PA265}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://africa-arabia-plate.weebly.com/ |title=African/Arabian Tectonic Plates |website=African/Arabian Tectonic Plates |access-date=2016-10-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.uwgb.edu/dutchs/GeolColBk/AfricanPlate.HTM |title=African Plate |website=Uwgb.edu |access-date=2016-10-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006145431/https://www.uwgb.edu/dutchs/GeolColBk/AfricanPlate.HTM |archive-date=6 October 2016}}</ref> However, for political and cultural reasons, maps generally display them as part of Europe instead.<ref name="hob">{{cite book |url=https://linguistics.stonybrook.edu/faculty/robert.hoberman/files/publications/Hoberman%202007%20Maltese%20morphology.pdf |page=257 |title=Chapter 13: Maltese Morphology |author=Robert D. Hoberman |publisher=Stony Brook University |location=Stony Brook, New York |access-date=26 July 2022}}</ref>

A single Spanish islet, known as [[Alboran Island]], is also debatably located on either the [[African Plate]] or the [[Eurasian Plate]].<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/2015JB012073 |title=Seismicity and active tectonics in the Alboran Sea, Western Mediterranean: Constraints from an offshore-onshore seismological network and swath bathymetry data |first1=Ingo |last1=Grevemeyer |first2=Eulàlia |last2=Gràcia |first3=Antonio |last3=Villaseñor |first4=Wiebke |last4=Leuchters |first5=Anthony B. |last5=Watts |date=17 December 2015 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |volume=120 |issue=12 |pages=8348–8365 |doi=10.1002/2015JB012073 |bibcode=2015JGRB..120.8348G |s2cid=54792160 |hdl=10261/127606 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> This island is located in the [[Alboran Sea]], 55&nbsp;km (34&nbsp;mi) north of the [[Morocco|Moroccan]] coast and 85&nbsp;km (53&nbsp;mi) south of [[Spain]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=La isla de Alborán {{!}} Patrimonio Natural |url=http://mediomarino.almediam.org/node/75# |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100616111816/http://mediomarino.almediam.org/node/75# |archive-date=2010-06-16 |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=mediomarino.almediam.org}}</ref>

===European-governed territories in Africa===
There are six definitive occurrences of territories unequivocally being a part of the African continent, but legally being administered by a [[European state]]. Three of these are administered by [[France]], and the other three by [[Spain]]. The existence of these territories further blurs the line between the borders of Africa and Europe, in particular with regard to the Spanish territories which lie immediately adjacent to and/or connected to the African mainland. The French territories lie within the [[Indian Ocean]], and, consequently, are more dislocated from the principal boundary between the two continents.{{cn|date=March 2026}}

The [[list of uninhabited regions|uninhabited]] Spanish [[unincorporated area|unincorporated]] overseas minor territories, known as the [[plazas de soberanía]] ("Localities of Sovereignty"),<ref>{{cite web|title=plaza #5 {{!}} Diccionario de la lengua española|url=https://dle.rae.es/plaza|last1=ASALE|first1=RAE-|last2=RAE|website=«Diccionario de la lengua española» - Edición del Tricentenario|language=es|access-date=2020-05-06}}</ref> are small islands that lie immediately adjacent to the North African coastline, with the exception of [[Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera]], which was originally an island like the other 'localities' but has subsequently become directly connected to the [[Morocco|Moroccan]] (African) mainland.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-10-26 |title=El histórico peñón español que un terremoto unió a la costa de Marruecos en 1930 |url=https://as.com/actualidad/sociedad/el-historico-penon-espanol-que-un-terremoto-unio-a-la-costa-de-marruecos-en-1930-f202510-n/ |access-date=2026-10-12 |work=Diario AS |language=es}}</ref> The two other Spanish territories are the exclaves of [[Ceuta]] and [[Melilla]], which are two populated coastal cities located directly on the African mainland, both bordering only Morocco.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cueto * |first=José Carlos |date=2022-05-20 |title=Por qué Ceuta y Melilla pertenecen a España si están en África |url=https://www.bbc.com/mundo/articles/cdj0xv1l8vro |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=BBC News Mundo |language=es}}</ref>

Two of the French territories are the inhabited [[overseas departments and regions of France|overseas departments and regions]] of [[Mayotte]] and [[Réunion]]. Mayotte is an island territory located west of the island country of Madagascar within the [[Mozambique Channel]]. Réunion is an island territory located near the island country of Mauritius and to the east of Madagascar (both nominally considered part of the African continent).<ref name="stats"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/mauritius/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109090348/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/mauritius |archive-date=9 January 2021 |title=Mauritius |date=2 March 2022 |publisher=Central Intelligence Agency |via=CIA.gov}}</ref> The final territory is the [[Scattered Islands in the Indian Ocean]], administratively a part of the [[French Southern and Antarctic Lands]]. This French territory consists of a range of minor uninhabited [[atoll]]s in the Indian Ocean, located in the deep sea surrounding Madagascar.{{cn|date=March 2026}}

==Antarctica==
Antarctica along with its outlying islands have no permanent population. All land claims south of 60°S latitude are held in abeyance by the [[Antarctic Treaty System]].{{cn|date=March 2026}}

Australia's [[Heard Island and McDonald Islands]] (an [[states and territories of Australia|external territory]]) and the French [[Kerguelen Islands]] are located on the [[Kerguelen Plateau]], on the [[Antarctic continental plate]]. Both are still within the bounds of the Indian Ocean. The United Nations categorizes Heard Island and McDonald Islands, which are politically affiliated with Australia, as being part of Oceania.<ref name="stats"/> The islands are 4,000 km from [[Perth]] in Australia, and have never been inhabited by [[indigenous peoples of Oceania]] or any other humans. Heard Island has only been visited 240 times throughout its entire history, and the [[McDonald Islands (Australia)|McDonald Islands]] have only ever been visited twice, in 1971 and 1980.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.traveller.com.au/australias-most-remote-territories-and-how-to-visit-them-12nz6m |title=Advance Australia far: Our most remote outposts |first=David |last=Whitley |date=14 January 2015 |website=Traveller}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ga.gov.au/scientific-topics/national-location-information/dimensions/remote-offshore-territories/heard-and-mcdonald-islands |title=Heard and McDonald Islands |first=c\=AU\;o\=Australia Government\;ou\=Geoscience |last=Australia |date=15 May 2014 |website=Ga.gov.au}}</ref> [[The World Factbook]] categorizes these islands as part of Antarctica rather than Oceania.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/heard-island-and-mcdonald-islands/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225224649/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/heard-island-and-mcdonald-islands/ |archive-date=25 February 2021 |title=Heard Island and McDonald Islands |date=21 June 2022 |publisher=Central Intelligence Agency |via=CIA.gov}}</ref>

The French [[Crozet Islands]], [[Île Amsterdam]], [[Île Saint-Paul]], and the Norwegian [[Bouvet Island]] are also located on the Antarctic continental plate, and are not often associated with other continents. The United Nations categorize Bouvet Island as part of South America,<ref name="stats"/> while the World Factbook categorizes it as part of Antarctica.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/bouvet-island/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117064829/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/bouvet-island/ |archive-date=17 January 2021 |title=Bouvet Island |date=6 June 2022 |publisher=Central Intelligence Agency |via=CIA.gov}}</ref>

[[South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands]] are closer to Antarctica than to any other continent. However, they are politically associated with the [[Falkland Islands]], which are less geographically isolated from South America. Furthermore, [[Argentina]], a South American country, maintains its [[irredentism|irredentist]] claims on all of these islands, which are administered by the [[United Kingdom]]. The United Nations consider them to be part of South America.<ref name="stats"/> Definitions of South America that exclude the [[Galápagos Islands]] and [[Juan Fernández Islands]] (both [[island#Geology|oceanic]] in nature) still generally include the Falklands, which share biographical affinities to [[Patagonia]] and [[Tierra del Fuego]], and which are located on the South American continental shelf.<ref name="sabirds">{{cite book |last1=S. Ridgely |first1=Robert |last2=Guy |first2=Tudor |title=The Birds of South America: Volume 1: The Oscine Passerines |date=1989 |publisher=University of Texas Press |page=14 |isbn=978-0-292-70756-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tRBb15pk4w0C&dq=%22SOUTH+GEORGIA%22+%22PART+OF+SOUTH+AMERICA%22&pg=PA14 |access-date=12 March 2022 |quote=Finally, a few comments on the area we consider to be part of "South America" are in order. Essentially we have followed the limits established by Meyer de Schauensee (1970: xii) with a few minor modifications. Thus, all the continental inshore islands ''are'' included (e.g., Trinidad and Tobago; various small islands off the northern coast of Venezuela, the Netherlands Antilles [Aruba, Bonaire, and Curaçao]; and Fernando de Noronha, off the northeastern coast of Brazil), but islands more properly considered part of the West Indies (e.g. Grenada) are ''not''. To the south, we have opted to include the Falkland Islands (or Islas Malvinas — in referring to them as the Falklands we are not making any political statement but merely recognizing that this book is being written in the English language), as their avifauna is really very similar to that of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. However, various other islands farther out in the South Atlantic (e.g., South Georgia) are not included except incidentally (e.g., endemic South Georgia Pipit have been incorporated). Likewise, the Juan Fernández Islands far off the Chilean coast have not been included (except for incidental comments), nor have the Galápagos Islands, situated even further off the Ecuadorian coast.}}</ref> The Falkland Islands and South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands were uninhabited when discovered by Europeans, with some theorizing that the Falklands were visited by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas]] during prehistoric times.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hamley |first1=Kit M. |last2=Gill |first2=Jacquelyn L. |last3=Krasinski |first3=Kathryn E. |last4=Groff |first4=Dulcinea V. |last5=Hall |first5=Brenda L. |last6=Sandweiss |first6=Daniel H. |last7=Southon |first7=John R. |last8=Brickle |first8=Paul |last9=Lowell |first9=Thomas V. |date=29 October 2021 |title=Evidence of prehistoric human activity in the Falkland Islands |journal=Science Advances |language=en |volume=7 |issue=44 |article-number=eabh3803 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.abh3803 |pmid=34705512 |pmc=8550247 |bibcode=2021SciA....7.3803H |issn=2375-2548}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=G. Hattersley-Smith |date=June 1983 |title=Fuegian Indians in the Falkland Islands |journal=[[Polar Record]] |volume=21 |issue=135 |pages=605–06 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/S003224740002204X |bibcode=1983PoRec..21..605H |s2cid=129083566}}</ref> These theories are usually considered dubious, as there is no archaeological evidence indicating prehistoric human inhabitation on the Falklands.<ref name="aljaz"/> South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands do not have any permanent residents. The Falkland Islands have historically had a [[British people|British]] population, with a culture distinct from that of mainland South America.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2013/03/falklands-rights-and-referendum-on-sovereignty-088584 |title=Falklands' rights and sovereignty |first=Sir Peter |last=Westmacott |website=POLITICO |date=7 March 2013}}</ref> There was [[Falklands War|a violent war]] between Argentina and the United Kingdom regarding ownership of the islands in 1982, and the residents of the Falklands do not currently wish to be associated with South America, despite their geographical proximity.<ref name="aljaz">{{cite web |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2007/4/1/uk-regrets-falklands-war-deaths |title=UK 'regrets' Falklands war deaths &#124; News |publisher=Al Jazeera |date=2007-04-01 |access-date=2022-03-09}}</ref>

The [[Prince Edward Islands]] are located between Africa and Antarctica, and are the territory of South Africa, an African country.{{cn|date=March 2026}}

[[Macquarie Island]] and the [[Antipodes Islands]], [[Auckland Islands]], and [[Campbell Islands]] are all uninhabited, and are located between Australia and New Zealand and Antarctica.<!-- see [[Talk:Transcontinental country#New Zealand|discussion]] --> The Antipodes Islands, Auckland Islands, and Campbell Islands are politically part of New Zealand, while Macquarie Island has been integrated into the Australian state of [[Tasmania]]. None are discrete political entities like Heard Island and McDonald Islands. As such, they are likely considered by the United Nations also to be part of Oceania. The Auckland Islands could be considered part of Oceania on cultural grounds rather than mere political grounds, as they are believed to be the southernmost island group to have been settled by [[Polynesians]] during prehistoric times.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/subantarctic-islands/page-4 |title=4. Early human settlement – Subantarctic islands |publisher=Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand |date=24 January 2013 |access-date=2 August 2013}}</ref> The islands were uninhabited when discovered by Europeans, but archaeological traces have since been found to indicate Polynesian settlement, dating to the 13th century, on Enderby Island. Macquarie Island is theorized to have possibly had contact with Polynesians, although there is no archaeological evidence to support this.<ref name="fr">{{cite web |url=https://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers19-08/010044590.pdf |title=Island locations and classifications |website=Horizon.documentation.ird.fr |access-date=29 December 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/history/stations/macquarie-island/ |title=Macquarie Island station: a brief history – Australian Antarctic Program |website=Antarctica.gov.au |date=7 August 2018 |access-date=29 December 2021}}</ref>

==Asia and Australia==
[[File:Map of Sunda and Sahul.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|The [[Wallace Line|Wallace]], [[Max Carl Wilhelm Weber|Weber]], and [[Richard Lydekker|Lydekker]] Lines, the three principal biogeographic boundaries in [[Wallacea]]]]

The continental boundary between Asia and [[Australia (continent)|Australia]] is somewhere in the [[Wallacea]]n region of the Malay Archipelago. The boundary is frequently divided along the anthropologic Melanesian Line or the biogeographic [[Max Carl Wilhelm Weber|Weber's Line]].{{citation needed|date=December 2020}} Geologically, the [[Aru Islands]] in [[Maluku Province]] and [[western New Guinea]], which contain six provinces of Indonesia, are part of the [[Australia (continent)|Australian continent]]. The eastern half of New Guinea is a part of [[Papua New Guinea]] which is considered part of Oceania.<ref name="stats"/> Indonesia is commonly referred to as one of the [[Southeast Asia]]n countries.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1355/9789814311175-016/pdf |doi=10.1355/9789814311175-016 |chapter=13. The Early Inscriptions of Indonesia and the Problem of the Sanskrit Cosmopolis |title=Early Interactions between South and Southeast Asia |year=2011 |pages=277–298 |publisher=ISEAS |isbn=978-981-4311-17-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1990/07/16/indonesias-new-economics-who-gains/8e3edd2b-6e71-4fe3-81e8-ec3b3cdf9b60/ |title=INDONESIA'S NEW ECONOMICS WHO GAINS? |date=1990-07-16 |author1=JACK ANDERSON |author2=DALE VAN ATTA |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |place=Washington, D.C. |issn=0190-8286 |oclc=1330888409}}</ref><ref name="handbook"/><ref name="stats"/> Indonesia's [[Eastern Indonesia|eastern]] region of Western New Guinea and nearby islands, makes it a transcontinental country; Western New Guinea is often considered part of Oceania because of its Indigenous [[Melanesians|Melanesian]] inhabitants and geological association with the Australian continental landmass.<ref name="devchris">{{cite book |doi=10.1002/9781118556115.ch44 |chapter=The Historical Development of Christianity in Oceania |title=The Wiley Blackwell Companion to World Christianity |year=2016 |last1=Ernst |first1=Manfred |last2=Anisi |first2=Anna |pages=588–604 |isbn=978-1-4051-5376-8}}</ref><ref name="asianpacific"/> [[East Timor]], an independent state that was formerly a part of Indonesia, is classified by the [[United Nations]] as a part of the [[United Nations geoscheme for Asia#South-eastern Asia|South-eastern Asia subregion]]. It has [[Accession of Timor-Leste to ASEAN|joined]] the [[ASEAN|Association of Southeast Asian Nations]],<ref name="ASEAN">{{cite web |title=Forging a New Era: Timor-Leste Admitted into ASEAN |url=https://asean.org/forging-a-new-era-timor-leste-admitted-into-asean/ |date=2025-10-26 |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=[[Association of Southeast Asian Nations|ASEAN]]}}</ref> having been involved as an ASEAN Regional Forum member since independence, and has participated in the [[Southeast Asian Games]] since [[2003 Southeast Asian Games|2003]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/postcolonial-blog/2019/nov/13/australias-history-with-east-timor-isnt-pretty-but-it-must-be-told-truthfully |title=Australia's history with East Timor isn't pretty but it must be told truthfully &#124; Paul Daley |date=13 November 2019 |website=The Guardian}}</ref>

Occasionally, all of the [[Malay Archipelago]] is included in Oceania, although this is extremely rare, especially as most of the archipelago lies on the [[Sunda Shelf|Asian continental shelf]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.skimountaineer.com/ROF/Region.php?region=Oceania |title=Skiing the Pacific Ring of Fire and Beyond: Oceania}}</ref> The Malay Archipelago was more frequently associated with Oceania during the 19th century, when the term was first coined.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cornell |first1=Sophia S. |title=Cornell's First Steps in Geography |date=1859 |publisher=The University of Michigan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wew1AQAAMAAJ&dq=%22malaysia+oceania%22&pg=PT1 |access-date=11 March 2022}}</ref><ref name="countriesoftheworld">{{cite book |last=Brown |first=Robert |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3-0DAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22oceania%22+%22juan%22+%22galapagos%22&pg=PA2 |title=The countries of the world |date=1876 |publisher=Oxford University |chapter=Oceania: General Characteristics |access-date=1 February 2022}}</ref> Many inhabitants in the Malay Archipelago are Austronesians, sharing genetic and linguistic affinities to the Melanesian, Micronesian, and Polynesian inhabitants of Oceania, who also fall under the Austronesian umbrella. However, the Austronesians of the Malay Archipelago had significant contact with mainland Asia during prehistoric times, unlike with the Austronesians and [[Indigenous Australian]]s of Oceania, who were isolated from the culture of Asia and the [[Eastern world]].<ref name="understanding"/> [[Epeli Hauʻofa]], a scholar of [[Tonga]]n and [[Fijians|Fijian]] descent, considered the Malay Archipelago separate from Oceania for this very reason. He wrote, "Before the advent of Europeans into the Pacific, our cultures were truly oceanic, in the sense that the sea barrier shielded us for millennia from the great cultural influences that raged through continental land masses and adjacent islands. This prolonged period of isolation allowed for the emergence of distinctive oceanic cultures with the only non-oceanic influences being the original cultures that the earliest settlers brought with them when they entered the vast, uninhabited region. Scholars of antiquity may raise the issue of continental cultural influences on the western and northwestern border islands of Oceania, but these are exceptions, and the Asian mainland influences were largely absent until the modern era. On the eastern extremity of the region there were some influences from the Americas, but these were minimal. It is for these reasons that Pacific Ocean islands from [[Japan]], through the [[Philippines]] and Indonesia, which are adjacent to the Asian mainland, do not have oceanic cultures, and are therefore not part of Oceania. This definition of our region delineates us clearly from Asia and the [[pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian Americas]] and is based on our own historical developments, rather than on other people's perceptions of us."<ref name="understanding">{{cite book |last1=Firth |first1=Stewart |last2=Naidu |first2=Vijay |title=Understanding Oceania: Celebrating the University of the South Pacific and its collaboration with The Australian National University |date=2019 |publisher=ANU Press |page=354 |isbn=978-1-76046-289-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cHmfDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22spread+of+our+islands+allowed+a+great+deal+of+mobility+within+the+region%22&pg=PA354}}</ref>

The United Nations and The World Factbook categorize the Australian [[Indian Ocean]] external territories of [[Christmas Island]] and [[Cocos (Keeling) Islands]] (both geographically adjacent to [[Java]]) as being part of Oceania, rather than Asia.<ref name="stats"/> The islands lie within the bounds of the [[Australian Plate]], and were uninhabited prior to European discovery in the 17th century. They have [[oceanic islands|oceanic geology]], making them distinct from both mainland Asia and mainland Australia.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ecat.ga.gov.au/geonetwork/srv/api/records/a05f7892-8f70-7506-e044-00144fdd4fa6 |title=BMR Cruise 107: Seabed Morphology and Offshore Resources around Christmas Island, Indian Ocean |website=Product catalogue}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://parksaustralia.gov.au/marine/pub/scientific-publications/archive/conservation-christmas-cocos.pdf |title=Conservation values in Commonwealth waters of the Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Island remote Australian territories |date=August 2009 |website=Parksaustralia.gov.au |access-date=26 July 2022}}</ref>

Japan possesses the [[Bonin Islands]] (also known as the Ogasawara Islands),<ref name="guamschool"/> the [[Volcano Islands]], and three remote islets ([[Nishinoshima (Ogasawara)|Nishinoshima]], [[Minami-Tori-shima]], and [[Okinotorishima]]), all governed collectively as [[Ogasawara, Tokyo|Ogasawara Village]], which is an [[administrative division]] consisting of scattered island [[atoll]]s located in the [[Pacific Ocean]]. These mostly uninhabited islands are located at some distance southeast of the [[Japanese archipelago]]. Owing to the location and oceanic nature of these islands, they are sometimes considered part of Oceania as well.<ref name="isl"/><ref name="global">{{cite web |title=Oceania Military Guide |url=https://www.GlobalSecurity.org/military/world/oceania/index.html |access-date=6 January 2022 |website=GlobalSecurity.org |publisher=[[Global Security]]}}</ref><ref name="realm">{{cite book |last1=Todd |first1=Ian |title=Island Realm: A Pacific Panorama |date=1974 |publisher=Angus & Robertson |page=190 |isbn=978-0-207-12761-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gcEJAQAAIAAJ&q=%22French+language+cultures%22+1974+pacific |access-date=2 February 2022 |quote=[we] can further define the word ''culture'' to mean ''language''. Thus we have the French language part of Oceania, the Spanish part, and the Japanese part. The Japanese culture groups of Oceania are the Bonin Islands, the Marcus Islands, and the Volcano Islands. These three clusters, lying south and south-east of Japan, are inhabited either by Japanese or by people who have now completely fused with the Japanese race. Therefore they will not be taken into account in the proposed comparison of the policies of non - Oceanic cultures toward Oceanic peoples. On the eastern side of the Pacific are a number of Spanish language culture groups of islands. Two of them, the Galapagos and Easter Island, have been dealt with as separate chapters in this volume. Only one of the dozen or so Spanish culture island groups of Oceania has an Oceanic population — the Polynesians of Easter Island. The rest are either uninhabited or have a Spanish - Latin - American population consisting of people who migrated from the mainland. Therefore, the comparisons which follow refer almost exclusively to the English and French language cultures.}}</ref><ref name="ausgov"/> The islands are within the [[Oceanian realm|Oceanian biogeographical realm]], unlike the rest of Japan,<ref name="class">{{cite web |last1=Udvardy |first1=Miklos D.F. |title=A Classification of the Biogeographical Provinces of the World |url=https://fnad.org/Documentos/A%20Classification%20of%20the%20Biogeographical%20Provinces%20of%20the%20World%20Miklos%20D.F.%20Udvardy.pdf |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=7 March 2022 |archive-date=4 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504205134/https://fnad.org/Documentos/A%20Classification%20of%20the%20Biogeographical%20Provinces%20of%20the%20World%20Miklos%20D.F.%20Udvardy.pdf}}</ref> and may have been inhabited by [[Micronesians]] around 2,000 years ago.<ref name="history"/> Their official discovery came much later in the 16th century, through Europeans.<ref name="guamschool">{{cite book |title=Oceania in the 21st Century - Color |date=2010 |publisher=St. John's School, Guam, USA |isbn=978-0-557-44505-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W1cudnPlxEsC&dq=%22oceania%22+%22bonin%22&pg=PA5 |access-date=12 March 2022 |quote=The Bonin Islands, now known as the Ogasawara Islands, are a group of subtropical islands located roughly equidistant between the Tokyo, Japan and the Northern Mariana Islands. This group of islands is nowhere near Tokyo, but it is still considered part of Tokyo! The Ogasawara Islands consist of 30 subtropical islands made The Bonin Islands were said to be discovered first by Bernardo de la Torre, a Spanish explorer, who originally called the islands "Islas del Arzobispo" [,,,]}}</ref><ref name="history">{{cite web |url=http://www.iwojima.jp/ogasa2.html |title=小笠原諸島の歴史 |website=Iwojima.jp}}</ref> The most remote island within this group, Minami-Tori-shima (also known as Marcus Island) is nearly 2,000 km removed from [[Tokyo]], and is geographically closer to the Micronesian territories of [[Guam]] and [[Northern Mariana Islands]].<ref name="guamschool"/><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.gsi.go.jp/common/000001188.pdf |title=Spatial Data Infrastructure Work in Japan 2000 − 2003 |journal=Bulletin of the Geographical Survey Institute |volume=50 |date=March 2004 |pages=9–25}}</ref> Inhabitants of the [[Ryukyu Islands]], on the periphery of the main Japanese archipelago, are sometimes associated with Austronesians.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/j.ctt1pwtd26.17.pdf |jstor=j.ctt1pwtd26.17 |chapter=The Ryukyu Islands and the Northern Frontier of Prehistoric Austronesian Settlement |last1=Hudson |first1=Mark J. |title=New Perspectives in Southeast Asian and Pacific Prehistory |year=2017 |volume=45 |pages=189–200 |publisher=ANU Press |isbn=978-1-76046-094-5}}</ref> The islands are geologically and historically linked with Asia, and are excluded from most definitions of Oceania, along with the similarly non-oceanic Japanese archipelago, which is not associated with Austronesians.<ref name="handbook"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Pandian |first1=Jacob |last2=Parman |first2=Susan |title=The Making of Anthropology: The Semiotics of Self and Other in the Western Tradition |date=2004 |publisher=Vedams |page=206 |isbn=978-81-7936-014-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RgO8nLql2KwC&dq=%22some+exclude+from+oceania%22&pg=PA206 |access-date=19 July 2022}}</ref> To the north of Japan is the disputed [[Kuril Islands]], currently administered by [[Russia]]. Usually, these islands are associated with the Russian [[Far East Asia|Far East]]. This is primarily as a result of their non-tropical biogeography, and their inhabitants, who are mostly [[Russians|ethnically Russian]] mainlanders.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SxBZAAAAYAAJ&q=%22aleutians%22+%22oceania%22 |title=Asia and the Americas |year=1943}}</ref>

Australia has a more developed economy than neighboring Pacific Island nations, and is occasionally associated with mainland Asia as a result of this, despite being geologically distinct and having no cultural links to it prior to European discovery. It has historically been included in definitions of Oceania, ever since the term was first coined in the early 1810s. In the 19th century, many geographers divided up Oceania into mostly racially-based subdivisions; ''Australasia'', ''Malaysia'' (encompassing the Malay Archipelago), ''Melanesia'', ''Micronesia'', and ''Polynesia''.<ref name="corn">{{cite book |last1=Cornell |first1=Sophia S. |title=Cornell's Primary Geography: Forming Part First of a Systematic Series of School Geographies |year=1857 |publisher=Harvard University |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1Z9hizT9tiAC&dq=%22included+in+oceania%22&pg=RA2-PA95 |access-date=31 March 2022 |archive-date=30 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220730064858/https://www.google.com.au/books/edition/CORNELL_S_PRIMARY_GEOGRAPHY/1Z9hizT9tiAC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22included+in+oceania%22&pg=RA2-PA95&printsec=frontcover |url-status=live}}</ref> Australia, Guam, and Northern Mariana Islands currently compete in the [[Asian Football Confederation]] (AFC), with Australia and Northern Mariana Islands having originally been part of the [[Oceania Football Confederation]] (OFC).<ref name="ofc">{{cite web |author=Admin |url=https://footballoceania.com/2021/02/03/the-curious-case-of-northern-mariana-islands-and-what-ofc-can-learn-from-it/ |title=The curious case of Northern Mariana Islands and what OFC can learn from it - Football in Oceania |website=Footballoceania.com |date=3 February 2021 |access-date=2022-03-09}}</ref> Guam was never an official OFC member, although they exclusively played against teams from Oceania prior to joining the AFC.<ref name="ofc"/> The presence of these teams in the AFC is not necessarily related to geography or politics, but rather because the Asian Football Confederation have far more resources than the Oceania Football Confederation.<ref name="ofc"/> All three are members of the [[Pacific Islands Forum]], the major governing body for the Oceania region, with Australia being a founding member in 1971. Guam and Northern Mariana Islands have had similar histories to the rest of [[Micronesia]], and are biogeographically and geologically distinct from mainland Asia.<ref name="pif">{{cite web |url=https://cooperation-regionale.gouv.nc/en/cooperation-pacific/pacific-islands-forum-pif |title=The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) &#124; Coopération Régionale et Relations Extérieures de la Nouvelle-Calédonie |website=Cooperation-regionale.gouv.nc |date=|access-date=2022-03-02}}</ref> [[Palau]] made an unsuccessful attempt to join the Asian Football Confederation in 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eaff.com/eanews/release/2009/090905.html |title=Regarding the agenda/ decisions of the 29th EAFF Executive Committee Meeting |access-date=27 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207081025/http://www.eaff.com/eanews/release/2009/090905.html |archive-date=7 February 2012}}</ref> They too share much of the same history as the rest of Micronesia, and are a member of the Pacific Islands Forum.<ref name="pif"/>

Taiwan has at times been associated with Oceania,<ref name="flick"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Marshall Cavendish Corporation |title=Encyclopedia of Earth and Physical Sciences: Nuclear physics-Plate tectonics |date=1998 |publisher=Pennsylvania State University |page=876 |isbn=978-0-7614-0551-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=px7YAAAAMAAJ&q=%22japan%22+%22aleutian%22+%22oceania%22 |access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref><ref name="ling">{{cite book |last1=Bowen |first1=James Dean |title=Linguistics in Oceania, 2 |date=1971 |publisher=The University of Michigan |page=|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lYouAAAAMAAJ&q=taiwan+Linguistics+in+Oceania+(2+v. |access-date=2 February 2022 |chapter=Japanese in Taiwan |quote=}}</ref><ref name="intmil">{{cite book |editor1-last=Dupuy |editor1-first=Trevor N. |title=International Military and Defense Encyclopedia: Volume 4 |date=1992 |publisher=The University of Michigan |page=2009 |isbn=978-0-02-881011-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wKYRAQAAMAAJ&q=%22taiwan+oceania%22 |access-date=19 March 2022 |quote=Despite varied usage, Ocean, from Madagascar off the coast of Africa to Taiwan, Oceania primarily refers to most of the thousands of islands in the Pacific Ocean, but not to the shore nations of its surrounding continents, or to the Japanese islands.}}</ref> not only because of their loose status as a Pacific Island, but also because of their [[Taiwanese indigenous peoples|indigenous population]], who are related to the natives of Oceania.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/travel/destinations/asia/67390585/new-zealands-long-lost-taiwanese-cuzzies |title=New Zealand's long-lost Taiwanese cuzzies |first=Adam |last=Dudding |date=15 March 2015 |website=Stuff}}</ref> In 2010, Australian historian [[Bronwen Phyllis Douglas|Bronwen Douglas]] claimed in ''The Journal of Pacific History'' that "a strong case could be made for extending Oceania to at least Taiwan, the homeland of the Austronesian language family whose speakers colonized significant parts of the region about 6,000 years ago."<ref>{{cite journal |title="Terra Australis" to Oceania: Racial Geography in the 'Fifth Part of the World' |author=Douglas, Bronwen |year=2010 |journal=The Journal of Pacific History |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=179–210 |doi=10.1080/00223344.2010.501696 |jstor=25764398 |pmid=20836257 |hdl=1885/52012 |s2cid=205438654 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Definitions of Oceania which include Taiwan are extremely rare because Taiwan has historical ties to mainland Asia, Taiwan is close to [[China]] (being 180 km away), and Taiwan lies on the continental shelf of Asia.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Oceania-region-Pacific-Ocean |title=Oceania &#124; Definition, Population, & Facts &#124; Britannica |website=Britannica.com}}</ref><ref name="intmil"/> Taiwan was formerly a member of the Oceania Football Confederation; this was for political reasons: It was forced to compete against teams from Oceania because China, its political administrator, did not recognize its sovereignty and would not compete against them. It was a member from 1975 to 1989, but now competes as part of the Asian Football Confederation.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.goal.com/en-au/news/chinese-taipei-india-intercontinental-cup-know-your-rivals/bugueu6dtcwd1u6nbyi6wmj90/match/4c8k8i08ssh8dc5lclsl4sxuy |title=Indian National Football Team: Know Your Rivals - Chinese Taipei |website=Goal.com}}</ref> Taiwan, Japan, and most of the nations in the Malay Archipelago are dialogue partners of the Pacific Islands Forum, but none have full membership; only Australia, New Zealand, and the island states in Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia do.<ref name="pif"/>

==<span class="anchor" id="Asia and Europe"></span><span class="anchor" id="Europe and Asia"></span>Asia and Europe==
The boundary between [[Asia]] and [[Europe]] is unusual among continental boundaries because of its largely mountain-and-river-based characteristics north and east of the Black Sea. Asia and Europe are considered separate continents for historical reasons; the division between the two goes back to the [[list of Graeco-Roman geographers|early Greek geographers]].{{cn|date=March 2026}}

In the modern sense of the term "continent", [[Eurasia]] is more readily identifiable as a "continent", and Europe has occasionally been described as a [[subcontinent]] of Eurasia.<ref name="europe">{{cite book |author=Hans Slomp |title=Europe: A Political Profile |year=2011 |publisher=Abc-Clio |isbn=978-0-313-39182-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LmfAPmwE6YYC&q=%22european+subcontinent%22&pg=PA634 |access-date=2014-09-10}}</ref>

===Mainland===

====History====
{{See also|Philip Johan von Strahlenberg#Von Strahlenberg's line|Greater Caucasus}}
[[File:Europe-geo.JPG|thumb|right|A French physical map of Europe from 1880, depicting the entirety of the [[Caucasus]] region as part of the European continent.<ref>Pierre Foncin. ''La deuxième année de géographie''. Edité par Armand Colin: 1880 </ref>]]
[[File:Eurasian borders.jpg|thumb|A map illustrating the evolving definition of the boundaries between Asia and Europe over the centuries. Line '''A''' (in red) used to be a widely accepted definition, but the most common definition in use today is Line '''B''' (for the east-west separation) and Line '''F''' (for the north-south separation), with the remaining definitions still being used on occasion.]]
[[File:Соловьёв (1874) p359.jpg|thumb|right|[[Russian Empire|Russian Imperial]] map of Europe from 1874, with an alternative southern limit at the Turkish border.]]

The threefold division of the [[Old World]] into Africa, Asia, and Europe has been in use since the 6th century BC by [[list of Graeco-Roman geographers|early Greek geographers]] such as [[Anaximander]] and [[Hecataeus of Miletus|Hecataeus]].<ref name="europe"/>

Anaximander placed the boundary between Asia and Europe along the [[Phasis River]] (the modern [[Rioni]] in [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] in the [[Caucasus Mountains]]), from Rioni mouth in [[Poti]] on the [[Black Sea]] coast, through the [[Surami Pass]] and along the [[Kura (Caspian Sea)|Kura River]] to the Caspian Sea, a convention still followed by [[Herodotus]] in the 5th century BC.
<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9FrGhw9TXn8C&q=phasis+border&pg=PA23 |title=A Culture of Freedom: Ancient Greece and the Origins of Europe |isbn=978-0-19-165240-0 |last1=Meier |first1=Christian |date=22 September 2011 |publisher=OUP Oxford}}</ref><ref>''[[Histories (Herodotus)|Histories]]'' 4.38. Cf. James Rennell, ''The Geographical System of Herodotus Examined and Explained'', Volume 1, Rivington 1830, [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_enQ-AAAAcAAJ/page/n274 <!-- quote=Herodotus Phasis. --> p. 244]</ref>
This convention was subsequently revised and the boundary between Asia and Europe was considered to be the [[Don River (Russia)|Tanais]] (the modern Don River).<ref>according to Strabo (''[[Geographica]]'' 11.7.4) at the time of [[Alexander the Great|Alexander]], "it was agreed by all that the Tanais river separated Asia from Europe" ({{lang|grc|ὡμολόγητο ἐκ πάντων ὅτι διείργει τὴν Ἀσίαν ἀπὸ
τῆς Εὐρώπης ὁ Τάναϊς ποταμός}}; cf. Duane W. Roller, ''Eratosthenes' Geography'', Princeton University Press, 2010, {{ISBN|978-0-691-14267-8}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=8peKyWK_SWsC&dq=Eratosthenes+Tanais&pg=PA57 p. 57])
</ref> This is the convention used by the Roman era authors [[Posidonius]],<ref>
W. Theiler, ''Posidonios. Die Fragmente'', vol. 1. Berlin: De Gruyter, 1982, fragm. 47a.</ref> [[Strabo]]<ref>
I.G. Kidd (ed.), ''Posidonius: The commentary'', Cambridge University Press, 2004, {{ISBN|978-0-521-60443-7}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=_iXs1aCr1ckC&q=Tanais&pg=PA738 p. 738].</ref> and [[Ptolemy]].<ref>
''[[Geography (Ptolemy)|Geographia]]'' 7.5.6 (ed. Nobbe 1845, [https://books.google.com/books?id=vHMCAAAAQAAJ vol. 2], p. 178)) {{lang|grc|Καὶ τῇ Εὐρώπῃ δὲ συνάπτει διὰ τοῦ μεταξὺ αὐχένος τῆς τε Μαιώτιδος λίμνης καὶ τοῦ Σαρματικοῦ Ὠκεανοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς διαβάσεως τοῦ Τανάϊδος ποταμοῦ.}}
"And [Asia] is connected to Europe by the land-strait between Lake Maiotis and the Sarmatian Ocean where the river Tanais crosses through."</ref>

Throughout the Middle Ages and into the 18th century, the traditional division of the landmass of [[Eurasia]] into two continents, Asia and Europe, followed Ptolemy, with the boundary following the [[Turkish Straits]], the [[Black Sea]], the [[Kerch Strait]], the [[Sea of Azov]], and the [[Don River (Russia)|Don]] (known in antiquity as the Tanais). But maps produced during the 16th to 18th centuries tended to differ in how to continue the boundary beyond the Don bend at [[Kalach-na-Donu]] (where it is closest to the Volga, now joined with it by the [[Volga–Don Canal]]), into territory not described in any detail by the ancient geographers.

[[Philip Johan von Strahlenberg]] in 1725 was the first to depart from the classical Don boundary by drawing the line along the [[Volga]], following the Volga north until the [[Samara Bend]], along [[Obshchy Syrt]] (the [[drainage divide]] between the [[Ural River|Ural]] and [[Volga]] rivers) and then north along the [[Ural Mountains]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Das Nord-und Ostliche Theil von Europa und Asia |author=Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg |year=1730 |language=de |page=106}}</ref><ref name="oren-icn.ru">{{cite web |url=http://oren-icn.ru/index.php/discussmenu/retrospectiva/685-eagraniza |title=Boundary of Europe and Asia along Urals |language=ru |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130417143618/http://oren-icn.ru/index.php/discussmenu/retrospectiva/685-eagraniza |archive-date=17 April 2013}}</ref> The mapmakers continued to differ on the boundary between the lower Don and Samara well into the 19th century. The [[:commons:Category:Atlas of Russian Empire. 1745 year|1745 atlas]] published by the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] has the boundary follow the Don beyond Kalach as far as [[Serafimovich (town)|Serafimovich]] before cutting north toward [[Arkhangelsk]], while other 18th- to 19th-century mapmakers such as [[John Cary]] followed Strahlenberg's prescription. To the south, the [[Kuma–Manych Depression]] was identified circa 1773 by a German naturalist, [[Peter Simon Pallas]], as a valley that, once upon a time, connected the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea,<ref name="oren-icn.ru"/><ref>Peter Simon Pallas, ''Journey through various provinces of the Russian Empire'', vol. 3 (1773)</ref> and subsequently was proposed as a natural boundary between continents.

By the mid-19th century, there were three main conventions, one following the Don, the [[Volga–Don Canal]] and the Volga, the other following the Kuma–Manych Depression to the Caspian and then the Ural River, and the third abandoning the Don altogether, following the [[Greater Caucasus watershed]] to the Caspian. The question was still treated as a controversy in geographical literature of the 1860s, with [[Douglas Freshfield]] advocating the Caucasus crest boundary as the best possible, citing support from various modern geographers.<ref>Douglas W. Freshfield, "[https://books.google.com/books?id=ips8AAAAIAAJ&dq=%22watershed+of+the+Caucasus%22&pg=PA71 Journey in the Caucasus]", ''Proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society'', Volumes 13-14, 1869.
Cited as de facto convention by Baron von Haxthausen, ''Transcaucasia'' (1854); review [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_SN0EAAAAQAAJ/page/n152 <!-- pg=140 quote="watershed of the Caucasus". --> Dublin University Magazine]</ref>

In Russia and the [[Soviet Union]], the boundary along the Kuma–Manych Depression was the most commonly used as early as 1906.<ref>[http://dlib.rsl.ru/view.php?path=/rsl01004000000/rsl01004103000/rsl01004103489/rsl01004103489.pdf#?page=163] {{dead link|date=August 2016}}</ref> Despite this, outside the geographical context, the territories of the North and South Caucasus were often classified as the European part of the country, for political, economic, and historical-cultural reasons.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.prlib.ru/en/node/454245 |title=European part of the USSR. Expeditions of 1931-1933. |language=en}}</ref> Thus, the political boundaries of Europe in the southern section were based on political and administrative borders. According to this principle, the extended boundary between Europe and Asia followed the state border of the USSR with Turkey and Iran (now it is the border from Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan).<ref>{{Citation |title=European U.S.S.R. and the Caucasus: 5-60 |date=1960-01-01 |url=https://www.loc.gov/resource/g7010.ct002952/ |access-date=2025-08-04 |others=United States |place=[Washington |language=english}}</ref> In 1958, the Soviet Geographical Society formally recommended that the boundary between Asia and Europe be drawn in textbooks from [[Baydaratskaya Bay]], on the [[Kara Sea]], along the eastern foot of the Ural Mountains, then following the [[Ural River]] until the [[Mugodzhar Hills]], and then the [[Emba River]]; and Kuma–Manych Depression,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://velikijporog.narod.ru/st_evraz_gran.htm |title=Do we live in Europe or in Asia? |language=ru}}</ref> thus placing the Caucasus entirely in Asia and the Urals entirely in Europe.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.i-u.ru/biblio/archive/orlenok_fisicheskaja/06.aspx |title=Physical Geography |year=1998 |author=Orlenok V. |language=ru |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111016212930/http://www.i-u.ru/biblio/archive/orlenok_fisicheskaja/06.aspx |archive-date=16 October 2011}}</ref> However, most geographers in the Soviet Union favoured the boundary along the Caucasus crest<ref>E. M. Moores, R. W. Fairbridge, ''Encyclopedia of European and Asian regional geology'', Springer, 1997, {{ISBN|978-0-412-74040-4}}, p. 34: "most Soviet geographers took the watershed of the Main Range of the Greater Caucasus as the boundary between Europe and Asia."</ref> and this became the standard convention in the latter 20th century, although the Kuma–Manych boundary remained in use in some 20th-century maps.

====Modern definition====
[[File:Pedestrian bridge in Orenburg.jpg|thumb|upright|Pedestrian bridge over the [[Ural River]] in [[Orenburg]] in [[Russia]]. The bridge is between [[Asia]] and [[Europe]]]]
[[File:On the bridge over Ural, Kizilskoe.jpg|thumb|Road sign on the continental border between Asia and Europe near [[Magnitogorsk]], Ural Mountains, Russia. It reads "Europe", above a crossed-out "Asia", as one enters Europe and leaves Asia]]

The modern border between Asia and Europe is a historical and cultural construct<ref>[[Encyclopædia Britannica]], [http://www.britannica.com/place/Asia Asia]:"The land boundary between Asia and Europe is a historical and cultural construct that has been defined variously; only as a matter of agreement is it tied to a specific borderline...", June 2021</ref> and, for that reason, its definition has varied. One commonly accepted border follows the [[Aegean Sea]], the [[Dardanelles]]–[[Sea of Marmara]]–[[Bosporus]] (together known as the [[Turkish Straits]]), the [[Black Sea]], along the [[drainage divide|watershed]] of the [[Greater Caucasus]], the northwestern portion of the [[Caspian Sea]], and along the [[Ural River]] and [[Ural Mountains]] to the [[Kara Sea]], as mapped and listed in most atlases including that of the [[National Geographic Society]] and as described in [[The World Factbook]].<ref name="NatlGeoAtlas">{{cite book |title=National Geographic Atlas of the World |edition=9th |year=2011 |location=Washington, DC |publisher=[[National Geographic Society|National Geographic]] |isbn=978-1-4262-0634-4}} "Europe" (plate 59); "Asia" (plate 74): "A commonly accepted division between Asia and Europe ... is formed by the Ural Mountains, Ural River, Caspian Sea, Caucasus Mountains, and the Black Sea with its outlets, the Bosporus and Dardanelles."</ref><ref name="Factbook">{{cite book |title=World Factbook |date=6 October 2021 |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/azerbaijan/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109221839/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/azerbaijan |archive-date=9 January 2021 |location=Washington, DC |publisher=[[Central Intelligence Agency]]}}</ref> According to this particular definition, [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] is a transcontinental country with some of its northern portions (such as [[Kazbegi Municipality]], [[Khevsureti]], and [[Tusheti]]) geographically located in [[Eastern Europe]], north of the [[Greater Caucasus#Watershed|Greater Caucasus Watershed]], whereas the country's south is arguably in Asia. Similarly, according to this one particular definition, [[Azerbaijan]] is a transcontinental country with some northern portions (e.g. [[Khachmaz District|Khachmaz]], [[Quba District (Azerbaijan)|Quba]], [[Qusar District|Qusar]], [[Shabran District|Shabran]], and [[Siazan District|Siazan]]) located north of the [[Greater Caucasus#Watershed|Greater Caucasus Watershed]] and thus geographically in Europe, whereas the rest arguably falls under Asia.<ref>{{cite book |title=World Factbook |date=6 October 2021 |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/azerbaijan/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109221839/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/azerbaijan |archive-date=9 January 2021 |location=Washington, DC |publisher=Central Intelligence Agency}} Azerbaijan: Geography and Georgia: Geography</ref> Georgia actively identified as European throughout the 19th and 20th centuries.<ref>{{cite web |title=Schuman Papers and Interviews: Georgia |url=https://www.robert-schuman.eu/en/european-issues/0674-georgia-terrible-dilemma-for-europe |access-date=2023-09-22 |website=robert-schuman.eu |language=}}</ref> In the 21st century, Georgia is regarded as a European country<ref>Encyclopedic World Atlas, George Philip & Son, [[Oxford University Press]]: 2002, [https://archive.org/details/encyclopedicworl0000geor/page/104/mode/2up p.104]</ref> for historical, cultural, religious, and political reasons.<ref>{{cite web |title=Country profiles |url=https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/country-profiles_en |website=european-union.europa.eu}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=EU relations with Georgia |url=https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/eastern-partnership/georgia/ |website=Consilium.europa.eu}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=4 July 2013 |title=10 things you might not know about Georgia |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-23072361}}</ref>

The international geographic community has never reached a universal agreement on continental borders, especially with regard to the Caucasus region between the Black and Caspian seas. As [[Encyclopædia Britannica]] explains:

<blockquote>
